newsitem.title: TAIWAN: YEAREND - Shipping deal still eludes Taiwan, China.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Shipping deal still eludes Taiwan, China.

text.p: Taiwan said in 1995 it would allow ships to sail directly between the island and the Chinese mainland. Arch-rival China in August this year announced its own rules on shipping links.
Both sides have yet to see eye to eye on direct shipping and the nearly five-decade ban preventing such links still stands.

However, analysts said China would have the upper hand with what it sees as a domestic shipping matter as Hong Kong, long a trading conduit for Taiwan and the Chinese mainland, returns to Beijing's rule in mid-1997.
"The bargaining chips are in China's hand," Chou Ho-ping, Dean of the College of Maritime Science at National Taiwan Ocean University, said in an interview.
China said on Friday that Taiwan ships which visit Hong Kong after June 30, 1997, must not fly any flag that contravenes Beijing's cherished "One China" principle.

Flying the Republic of China flag used by Taipei is banned in China, which has considered Taiwan a rebel province since the defeated Nationalist government fled to the island at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
Taiwan has banned all direct contact with China from that time and trade with the mainland must be routed through a third region. Most go through Hong Kong.
But since a political thaw started in the late 1980s, Taiwan has been exploring ways to ease the ban, provided that any such move would not undermine the island's security.

More than 25,000 Taiwanese firms have poured over US$20 billion into China since the late 1980s, increasing pressure on the Taiwan government to meet economic demands from businessmen but, at the same time, avoid overdependence on China.

Transshipping across the Taiwan strait has soared in recent years and cargo shipped directly from Taiwan to the mainland would save 40 percent from the cost of shipping through Hong Kong, Taiwan's transport vice minister, Mao Chi-kuo, has estimated. "We estimate that direct shipping links with China will save Yang Ming U$26.18 million a year," said Frank Lu, president of Taiwan's shipping giant Yang Ming Marine Corp.

Bowing to pressure from businessmen, Taiwan said in 1995 that it would allow limited direct shipping links with China under Taipei's "offshore transshipment centre" plan, but the project has been delayed by sovereignty issues.
Under that plan, "feeder vessels" below a certain tonnage would be allowed to make direct crossings, bringing cargoes to ocean-going ships berthed in mainland or Taiwan harbours.

In November this year, Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui approved a scheme that allowed foreign-flagged ships to sail directly aross the strait, a move which officials called a refinement of the 1995 plan.
But it remains a question whether China will allow those direct crossings to begin.
Semi-official talks between the two long-time rivals have been suspended by an angry Beijing since President Lee's private but high-profile visit to the United States in mid-1995.
Beijing saw Lee's trip as a move to promote Taiwan's independence.

Ignoring the political impasse, Taiwan gave a cool response when China unveiled unilateral rules governing direct shipping links with Taiwan in August, saying Beijing's rules were "mingled with sensitive political issues".
Saying Hong Kong's transshipment centre role would remain after the 1997 handover, Taipei has also been seeking substitutes as the territory's return to China tangled with political concerns.
Taiwan fears that Beijing could exploit Taipei's heavy reliance on the territory and squeeze it for political concessions.
Beijing has already decreed that shipping and air links between Hong Kong and Taiwan can continue after the handover of the colony after more than 150 years of British rule.
President Lee has expressed concern at an overdependence on China's economy, calling for a slowdown in investments there.
But Taiwan shipping operators still want direct links.
Yang Ming said it planned to open five offices in China to cope with rising business brought by expected direct shipping links.
A group of local shipping firms set up a Taiwan Strait Shipping Association in August, hoping to bring an end to the ban on direct shipping links through contacts at civilian level.
However, as there is no indication of a resumption of semi-official talks between the two sides, shipping operators might have to wait longer than they hope.

Chiang Ping-kun, chairman of Taiwan's Council for Economic Planning and Development, said in November that China would have no political interest in resuming dialogue before Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule.
